vignette:
He is 18, originally from an African immigrant family, and works as a junior tax consultant in a small accounting office where he is known for being quiet, precise, and unusually serious for his age. When he first talks about what happened, he does so in fragments, as if the story belongs to someone else. He says there was a client event after the end of tax season, a gathering his supervisor encouraged everyone to attend. He had wanted to make a good impression. He stayed later than he meant to, accepted a ride from an older acquaintance connected to the office, and remembers trying to ignore the first sense that something was wrong. He recalls the smell of the car, the sound of the locks, the pressure of being trapped between wanting to stay polite and knowing he was no longer safe. When he describes the assault, his voice becomes flat. He remembers freezing, hearing himself say “stop” as if from very far away, and then hating himself afterward for not fighting harder.

In the days that follow, he tells no one. He goes to work on Monday in the same shirt and tie he had laid out the night before the event, determined to prove that nothing has changed. He sits at his desk reviewing returns, checking figures again and again because he cannot hold a line of numbers in his mind without suddenly seeing the inside of the car. When colleagues ask if he is tired, he says he is just busy. He avoids looking at the man’s email address when it appears in the office inbox and feels a sharp wave of nausea whenever a phone buzzes unexpectedly. At home, he showers for a long time and scrubs his skin until it hurts. He begins sleeping in short bursts, waking with his heart pounding and the certainty that someone is in the room. Some nights he does not sleep at all, instead sitting upright with the light on, listening for footsteps.

Over the next months, his world becomes smaller. He changes his route to work to avoid the street where he had been dropped off that night. He stops attending office lunches and leaves as soon as the workday ends. He had once imagined building a future in finance, maybe studying further, maybe opening his own firm one day. Now his attention narrows to getting through each hour without feeling overwhelmed. When a male client leans too close over his desk to point out a number on a form, he goes rigid. His chest tightens, his ears ring, and for a moment he is no longer in the office. He starts making excuses to work in the records room where no one bothers him. If someone comes up behind him unexpectedly, he flinches so hard he knocks over a stack of files.

He feels ashamed in ways he struggles to put into words. He worries that being assaulted means something about him that others will see immediately. He is terrified that if he tells anyone, they will laugh, question him, or decide he must have wanted it. In his family and community, he has grown up with strong ideas about masculinity, respect, and silence. He carries those expectations heavily. He tells himself other men survive worse. He says he should be able to “move on.” Instead he finds himself checking doors repeatedly, scanning every room for exits, and sitting only where he can see who is entering. He no longer plays football with friends and stops answering messages. When his mother asks why he is losing weight, he says work is stressful.

The memories intrude without warning. A cologne similar to the perpetrator’s makes his stomach drop. The click of a car lock can leave him trembling. Sometimes, while reviewing spreadsheets, he loses several minutes staring at the screen, frozen and far away. Other times he is irritable and explosive over small mistakes, then disgusted with himself afterward. He feels detached from everyone, even when sitting among people he loves. On his worst days he looks at his reflection and feels as if he is seeing a stranger—someone weak, dirty, permanently altered.

By the time he speaks openly in therapy, he is exhausted by the effort of appearing functional. He is still going to work, still meeting deadlines, still dressing carefully each morning, and from the outside his life looks intact. But he lives in a constant state of alarm. He dreads the dark, avoids intimacy of any kind, and trusts no one easily. He says the hardest part is that the assault did not stay in one night; it keeps happening in pieces—in his sleep, on the bus, at his desk, in the silence just before he opens his front door. He misses the version of himself who could laugh easily, who could focus on numbers without fighting panic, who believed that hard work made the world predictable. Now each day is organized around not remembering, and around the fact that remembering comes anyway.
